title: The single life
hook: single people also live a calling of love and service

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage as calling: the couple giving the sacrament to each other, and Paul's great sacrament. Your line was holy through each other. Whose day did your unasked kindness touch? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

A question single people sometimes get at family weddings: so, when's it your turn? Asked kindly, over cake, as if life were a waiting room and the real thing starts at the altar. Meanwhile, look at the week of one single man. Tuesday, he drives his elderly neighbor to the cardiologist. Wednesday, he's the one his sister calls at midnight. Saturday, he coaches a team of nine-year-olds who think he's the funniest man alive. Sunday, he reads at the early Mass. Nobody at the wedding asked about any of that. Today, the single life.
screen: `WHEN'S IT YOUR TURN?` → `A WEEK OF ONE SINGLE MAN.` → `NOBODY ASKED ABOUT THAT.`

segments.voice: Start with something easy to skip: the Gospels give Jesus no wife. Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul. And Paul writes about it to the church in Corinth with real warmth. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I would that all men were even as myself: but every one hath his proper gift from God; one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift. Marriage is a gift; so is the unmarried life. Then he adds why it matters: "He that is without a wife, is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please God." The unmarried person, Paul says, has room. Room for prayer, for friends, for people who need someone to show up. The Catechism speaks to single people directly. It says that many live single not by their own choice, because of the circumstances of their lives, and that they are especially close to the heart of Jesus. It asks parishes to open their doors to them, and it says that no one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone. So the Catholic picture isn't of a person waiting for a vocation to begin. The call to holiness from two days ago is already theirs, whole. Some single people take a vow later, some marry later, and some live single all their lives. None of those seasons is a gap in the calling. Love and service don't need a ring to count. The neighbor at the cardiologist knows that.
screen: `THE GOSPELS GIVE JESUS NO WIFE.` · `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT.` · `ROOM FOR THE THINGS OF THE LORD.` · `THE CHURCH IS A HOME FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT FROM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a single friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know who is single. A friend, an aunt, a coworker, a widower down the street, or yourself. Think of one specific way they show up for people. Let that picture be clear: the drive, the call, the meal. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name, and ask that they be loved as they love. If you don't, simply let gratitude for them fill the sit. The bell holds the time.
The single life. In Catholic teaching, a life lived unmarried, by choice or by circumstance, that is already a whole calling to love and service. Today's word.
Your line: a whole calling. Today, tell one single friend, in a text or in person, one specific thing they do that you've noticed and are glad of. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Single Catholics live the call to holiness in their work, friendships, family and parish, without vows of religious life. The Catechism asks parishes to welcome single people and describes the Church as a home and family for everyone.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 7:7 and 7:32: confirm exactly.
'Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul' leans on 1 Corinthians 7:7–8; some readers argue Paul was a widower. Phrased cautiously; confirm.

CCC 1658 (single persons, often not of their choosing, especially close to Jesus' heart; the doors of homes and parishes open to them; 'no one is without a family in this world') paraphrased; confirm. The Catechism says 'great number'; the script says 'many', which the text supports.
Greek ἄγαμος in 1 Corinthians 7:32: confirm spelling and pronunciation.
The hook's single man is an illustrative scene, not a real person.
Editor: 'Jesus never married' restated as what the Gospels show.
